children: By Anoop Menon

About 4.6 million square metres (sqm) of organised retail space could be added across the GCC between 2025 and 2030, assuming 80% of projected additions are completed, according to investment banking advisory firm Alpen Capital.

This would increase total organised retail gross leasable area (GLA) to 27 million sqm, representing a CAGR of 3.8 percent over the period, the UAE-based firm said in the 10th edition of its GCC Retail Industry report issued on Wednesday.
Physical retail continues to attract investment despite the growth of e-commerce, Hameed Noor Mohamed, Managing Director of Alpen Capital (ME) told Zawya Projects.
He said continued investment in new malls across the UAE, Saudi Arabia and other GCC markets indicates that physical retail remains an important part of the sector despite changing purchasing habits.
“End of the day, consumers need to look at the goods or to have an experience,” he said.
The report estimates total GCC retail sales at $329.6 billion in 2025, falling 3 percent to $319.8 billion in 2026, before recovering to $362.0 billion in 2028 and $386.9 billion by 2030.

Alpen Capital forecasts retail sales to grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 3.3 percent across 2025-2030. The UAE is expected to record the fastest growth among GCC countries, with a CAGR of 3.6 percent.
Mohamed said the firm lowered its initial growth projections to account for the impact of the current conflict on supply chains and logistics.
“We have taken the current scenario and tweaked the model around that,” he said. “If the war was not there, probably the projections would have been much better.
He added that the firm has forecasted the sector to grow despite the disruption.
Retailers are responding differently to higher logistics and supply-chain costs, with some absorbing the increases and others passing part of them on to consumers, said Mohamed.
If the disruption persists, he expects the additional costs to be shared between retailers and consumers, depending on the product category.
He expects retail margins to normalise over the medium term as competition limits companies' ability to maintain higher prices once logistics costs decline.

According to the report, macroeconomic conditions, government initiatives and a recovery in consumer spending is expected to return the sector to steady growth. Population growth, rising spending power and economic diversification are expected to support the sector, alongside the expansion of e-commerce and omnichannel retail and the entry and expansion of international and domestic brands.
The UAE is expected to record the fastest growth among GCC countries, with retail sales increasing at a CAGR of 3.6 percent over the forecast period,
Funding remains available
Financing conditions for retail projects remain supportive despite geopolitical uncertainty, with banks continuing to lend to viable developments, Mohamed said.
“There is liquidity available, the market is comfortable, and if it's a good project, loans are being given,” he said.
The cost of finance has also remained relatively stable, with banks generally supporting customers rather than tightening lending sharply in response to the conflict, he said.
Furthermore, the 25-basis-point Federal Reserve rate hike is marginal in the overall scheme of things in the Gulf and unlikely to impact borrowers significantly.
Private credit interest
Outside traditional banking channels, private credit could emerge as an alternative source of financing in the GCC, although the market remains relatively nascent, according to Mohamed.

He pointed out that large global funds typically seek sizable transactions, with ticket sizes potentially in the $50 million to $100 million range, limiting the number of GCC retail projects currently suitable for such financing.
“A private credit fund is happy take high risk but with high returns,” he said,

Mohamed said Alpen is well connected with large private credit funds from markets including Europe, Singapore and India at opportunities in the region, including transactions that may not meet traditional bank lending criteria.
He expects the market to broaden as more private credit providers coming to the region look at potentially smaller ticket sizes.
“This is the trend where the market is moving towards,” he said. “It's already moved in this direction in other markets, and it's just a matter of time before it comes here.”
(Reporting by Anoop Menon; Editing by SA Kader)
